newsitem.title: USA: Democrats try to block tobacco liability limits.
newsitem.headline: Democrats try to block tobacco liability limits.

text.p: Three Democratic senators said Thursday they would try to change a product liability bill so it would not give the tobacco industry an escape hatch from financially painful terms of a possible settlement of state lawsuits.
"There is a card up the industry's sleeve," said Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat. "We will fight a bailout for the tobacco industry."

Lautenberg and two fellow Democrats, Richard Durbin of Illinois and Ron Wyden of Oregon, said they would introduce an amendment to the product liability bill to make clear that tobacco would not be eligible for proposed caps on punitive damages in the bill.
However they acknowledged that at this point no Republican senators have endorsed their proposal although at least 16 state attorneys general have.
Liability limits are a contentious issue in settlement talks under way between the industry and the three dozen states suing them.

Many public health experts and Congressional critics of the industry say they cannot endorse a settlement if there are limits to what tobacco victims can recover. But Lautenberg warned that the product liability bill, which is separate from any possible legislation that Congress would have to enact to facilitate a tobacco settlement, gives the industry a back door out.
Also in Congress Thursday, Sen. Gordon Smith, an Oregon Republican, and Rep. Sanford Bishop, a Georgia Democrat, said they were introducing a bill to crack down on teen-age smoking.

It would penalize states that did not enact a model law that imposes fines both on businesses that sell cigarettes to minors as well as to to the youths themselves, who could also risk having their drivers' licenses suspended.

In some ways their plan goes further than the new Food and Drug Administration regulations, which do not penalize youths. However, the proposal does not have as strict limits on vending machines, does not have the mandatory I.D. checks for anyone who looks under age 27 and does not address the issue of advertising in youth markets.
